newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's CADES to show accounting surplus in 1997.
newsitem.headline: France's CADES to show accounting surplus in 1997.

text.p: French welfare debt repayment fund CADES will show an accounting surplus next year which will be used in the calculation of France's total public sector borrowing requirement, a government official said on Tuesday.
The surplus would help the government's efforts to reduce the total public sector borrowing requirement, as defined by the Maastricht treaty, to three percent of gross domestic product.
Next year is the crucial year for deciding which countries are eligible to join European monetary union in 1999.
The official declined all comment on the likely size of the surplus, which will effectively represent revenues raised by CADES minus interest payments due.
CADES is expected to raise some 25 billion francs next year from the proceeds of a flat 0.5 percent tax on most income, the RDS (Remboursement de la Dette Sociale).

This 25 billion is meant to cover interest payments due plus capital repayments. But while interest payments will be accounted as current spending, capital repayments on existing debt will not -- therefore leaving an accounting surplus.
Economists said it was difficult to calculate the size of the likely surplus, given that CADES had not yet decided how to structure its borrowings next year.
CADES has yet to decide how much to finance at floating rates and fixed rates and on a profile of its debt repayments.

But as a very rough estimate, CADES has taken on total welfare debt of some 250 billion francs -- covering repayment of interest and principle on 110 billion francs of welfare debt run up to the end of 1993 and on 140 billion of welfare debt run up in 1994 and 1995 -- to be repaid over 13 years.
Assuming average interest rates of six percent -- the current rate on seven-year government issues -- interest payments on 250 billion francs would total 15 billion.
That would leave 10 billion extra from the total 25 billion to be raised next year to be marked down as an accounting surplus.
Financial daily Les Echos earlier on Tuesday cited a figure of 10 billion as the likely CADES surplus.

The government is due to present a budget for 1997 on September 18, at which time it has promised to explain how it plans to reduce the total public sector borrowing requirement to three percent of GDP from a targeted four percent this year and five percent last year.
